title: Syllabus
text:
This course introduces quantitative research methods to study questions from international relations and European politics, using modern tools for scientific programming and reproducible research. You will learn to analyse and visualise data in R, document your work in Quarto, and manage your projects with Git and GitHub. Together these tools support state-of-the-art workflows for transparent, collaborative and well-organised empirical research. All work is done in Positron, an integrated development environment for data science.
In this course, we will learn the regression paradigm as a general framework for modeling patterns in data – essentially, fitting lines and curves to describe relationships among variables – and Bayesian inference as a framework for quantifying uncertainty and learning efficiently from data.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course objectives
The overall goal is to give you the practical skills and the methodological confidence to write an empirical bachelor thesis in political science. You will learn to preprocess data, choose and implement appropriate models for continuous and binary outcomes, compute quantities of interest, and interpret results substantively.
Beyond technical proficiency, the course emphasises sound statistical reasoning, effective data visualisation, and communicating empirical findings clearly to a non-technical audience. Through weekly assignments and a cumulative take-home exam, you will develop the ability to evaluate statistical claims critically in academic research and in public debate alike.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course logistics

General information
The course meets on Wednesdays, 13:45-15:15, in A5, 6 – C 108. Each session consists of an instructor-led part on concepts and theory, followed by hands-on exercises. Homework is assigned at the end of class and is due 7 days later, before the next session. Readings provide background, theory and context, and are linked per week from the Schedule.






Tip



If you have to miss a session, tell me beforehand. Email me before the session and I will set up a Zoom room so you can follow it remotely.




Prerequisites
Two different things go by this name, and it is worth keeping them apart. The first is an administrative condition on taking the module. The second is what you need on day one to follow what happens in the room.
Formally. The module requires the Basismodul Einführung in die Internationalen Beziehungen and the Basismodule in Methoden und Statistik. Whether you meet those is a question for the module catalogue and the Studienbüro, not for me.
In terms of what this course assumes: nothing. No programming experience is assumed, and no statistics beyond descriptive measures. Everything the course needs, it teaches.
A basic grasp of statistics does help, and if you would like to shore that up before or during the term, Section 3.12 points at two free ways to do it.


Module, credits and workload

Module: Advanced Module: International Relations
This course: Methods exercise class (Übung)
Credits: 6 ECTS, which is 180 hours of total workload
Recommended semester: 5th Semester
Contact time: 19.5 hours, that is 13 sessions of 90 minutes
Self-study: 160.5 hours, about 12.3 hours a week across the 13 teaching weeks

That self-study figure is not decoration. It is where the weekly homework, the readings and your exam preparation actually live, and the course is paced on the assumption that you spend roughly that much time on it.
For comparison, the module catalogue budgets a nominal 30 hours of contact time and 150 hours of self-study for a 6 ECTS course. The difference is simply that this course meets for 90 minutes over 13 weeks rather than for the nominal figure, so a little more of the same total lands outside the room.
The authoritative version of all of these is the module catalogue and the examination regulations for the B.A. Political Science, not this page. Where the two disagree, the regulations win.


Attendance policy
Active participation (Mitarbeit) is a required component of the coursework (Studienleistung), on the basis of section 13b of the examination regulations. This course consists of 13 sessions. Successful participation is presumed if you attend at least 80% of sessions, that is at least 11 out of 13.
If attendance falls below 80% but stays at or above 60% (8 to 10 out of 13), successful participation is not presumed. In that case the possibility of fulfilling the participation requirement is assessed case by case.
If attendance falls below 60% (fewer than 8 out of 13), successful participation is normally considered impossible under the examination regulations.
If sessions are cancelled during the semester, the absolute number of required sessions is adjusted accordingly, while the percentage thresholds stay unchanged.


Grading policy
Under the examination regulations, assessment consists of coursework (Studienleistung, pass or fail) and a final examination (Prüfungsleistung, graded).
Successful completion of all coursework requirements is a prerequisite for admission to the final take-home exam.

Coursework (Studienleistung, pass or fail)
Coursework has two components, and both must be passed. This is the model the module catalogue provides for rather than a local invention: it names Mitarbeit and Hausaufgaben among the Studienleistungen for this course.
1. Weekly homework assignments. There are 11 homework assignments over the term, one in every session except the first and the last. The first session is orientation and the last is synthesis and the exam briefing, so neither sets work, which leaves weeks 2 to 12. They are distributed through GitHub and assessed pass or fail. To fulfil this requirement you must pass at least 80% of them, that is 9 out of 11. Homework must show a serious and complete attempt at the tasks. A submission that is empty or clearly insufficient does not count as passed.
2. Active participation (Mitarbeit). Active participation, as described in Section 3.4, is a required coursework component and is assessed pass or fail.



The take-home exam
The final examination (Prüfungsleistung) is a take-home exam, and it determines the whole course grade. In the module catalogue it goes by its formal name, a written term paper (schriftliche Hausarbeit). Those are two names for the same thing.
Window: 9 December 2026, 15:30 to 23 December 2026, 23:59.
It is distributed through the exam repository on the course GitHub organisation, the same template flow as the weekly homework. The last version pushed to your exam repository before the deadline is what gets graded. Late submissions are not accepted.
What you receive. A dataset, the theoretical background you need, and a small number of stated hypotheses. You do not have to find a topic, a question or data of your own.
What you produce. A short empirical research report that tests those hypotheses using the eight-step Bayesian workflow in Section 6. The rendered PDF follows the structure of an empirical political science paper: a data and methods (or research design) section, a results (or analysis) section, a discussion including limitations, and a brief conclusion. No introduction and no literature review are required, because the background and hypotheses are given to you.

The report may not exceed 6,000 words. That limit is set by the module catalogue, not by me. The reference list, the appendices and the statutory declaration do not count towards it, which is my clarification rather than the catalogue’s.
Use figures and tables wherever they genuinely support the argument.
Do not print raw code, warnings, messages or unformatted R output in the PDF.
Appendices are welcome for diagnostics, robustness checks and supporting material that is not essential to the main text.

What you submit.

firstname_lastname_exam.qmd and the rendered firstname_lastname_exam.pdf, at the root of your exam repository.
The whole repository, which is part of the submission. Any further notebooks or scripts are inspected and count towards the grade. Treat it as a research project.
A signed statutory declaration on the final page of the PDF, following the university’s template. An electronic signature is fine. A PDF without one cannot be graded.

How it is graded. On the university scale, 1.0 (very good) to 5.0 (insufficient), across the four dimensions in Table 1. The full criterion-by-criterion scheme, which is what you should actually work from, is distributed together with the exam.



Table 1: The four grading dimensions of the take-home exam and their weights. Argumentation, Interpretation and Formalities are assessed from the rendered PDF alone, so a justification that lives only in a code comment does not count. Code and repository is assessed from the repository as a whole.










Dimension
What it asks
Points




Argumentation
Are your modelling choices reasoned and justified in the PDF, given the data and the hypotheses?
30


Interpretation
Are your posterior results read correctly and used to evaluate the hypotheses?
30


Formalities
Does the PDF look and read like a section of a published paper?
15


Code and repository
Is the workflow operationalised in a reproducible, traceable repository?
25


Total

100












Important



A submission that does not render from a clean clone cannot reach top marks. The single largest criterion in the code and repository dimension is that the PDF rebuilds from your repository on another machine. Test that before the deadline, not after.


Every tool and workflow the exam needs is taught during the course. Session 12, the multilevel primer, is the one exception: it is not examined.


Registration and withdrawal
Registration for the Prüfungsleistung, deregistration, and the applicable deadlines are handled by the Studienbüro under the examination regulations, not by me. Check the dates there and keep to them, because responsibility for meeting them sits with you.
If a good reason, illness in particular, prevents you from completing the exam within the window, section 30 of the examination regulations applies. You must submit a written application to the Studienbüro without delay, with evidence. The examination board decides, and the burden of proof is on the applicant. Tell me as well, but telling me is not a substitute for the formal application.
Section 5 additionally allows the deadlines for coursework and examinations to be extended on a timely written application, for instance for students with children or with dependants requiring care.


Disability and chronic illness
If a disability or a chronic illness makes it harder for you to take an assessment in the form it is set, you are entitled to compensation that restores equal opportunity, under section 6 of the examination regulations. Applications are made in writing and in good time, and applications on grounds of disability or chronic illness go to the university’s representative for students with disabilities or chronic illness.






Tip



Talk to me early, and tell me only what you want to. The formal route runs through the representative and the examination board, and I do not need to know the nature of your condition. What helps me is knowing early that an adjustment is coming, so it can be built in rather than improvised.




Language and software policy
The course is taught entirely in English and is built around R, Quarto and Git or GitHub for data analysis, reproducible research and project management. Work with these tools, because the exercises and workflows are designed around them.
For the take-home exam you may use another script-based language such as Python or Stata, but this is not recommended and no guidance is provided for non-R workflows. The emphasis is on understanding the tools, practising them, and learning to find solutions independently.


Hardware
You need a computer available during class. A standard laptop is sufficient, and there are no particular requirements for RAM, an external GPU, or other advanced components.
If you do not own a suitable device, the University of Mannheim IT department offers a laptop rental service. Please make use of it if you need it.


Software
Install all required software before the first session, following the separate installation guide. Doing it early means we can sort out any problems on day one and start the programming work properly in the following session.


Additional learning resources
Two external platforms are worth your time. Both are voluntary and neither is part of the requirements to pass, but each fills a gap this course cannot fill on its own in one session a week.
DataCamp. Use the link to join the course group, which gives you six months of premium access. DataCamp offers in-depth, self-paced practical training in R, coding, data analytics and AI topics, so it is the right place to drill something until it is automatic, at whatever speed suits you. The introduction to R track is a good starting point.






Warning



Register with your uni-mannheim.de address. Premium access is tied to the university account. If you sign up with a private address the group link will not grant it, and the fix is to start again with the right address.


Duolingo Math. Freemium, and a good starting point if you would like to relaunch yourself into mathematics fundamentals or introductory statistics. No prior statistics is assumed in this course, so this is not a prerequisite. It is simply there if the maths behind a session feels shakier than you would like.


Mental health support
Life and study at the University of Mannheim can sometimes feel complicated, challenging, or overwhelming. That is completely normal. You are not expected to understand or memorise course content on the first attempt.
If you ever feel mentally or emotionally strained, you may find useful advice on the university’s good mental health and studying page. The help in times of crisis page gives an overview of the counselling and support services available at the university.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI policy
All submissions are checked for plagiarism, and violations of the code of conduct may result in failing the course or in expulsion.

AI is encouraged
You will use AI tools during this course. That is a prediction, not a guess, and pretending otherwise would produce a policy nobody follows. So the question here is not whether but how to make AI use visible and trustworthy.






Tip



Use it, and think of it as a tutor. Always available, infinitely patient, and no question is too basic. Lean on it when you are stuck, to explain a concept, to tidy code, to improve your writing. You take final responsibility for everything you submit.


Two honest caveats. First, AI is more reliable on formal logic, programming and well-covered general topics than on narrow substantive questions in international relations, so treat narrow factual claims sceptically and check the source. Second, leaning on it before you understand the material does hinder learning: research suggests AI helps most those who already understand the topic. For a fuller explanation of why AI can undermine learning, see this piece by Andrew Heiss. Do the thinking first, then let the tool help.


Say so in the commit message
This course asks for one thing in return, and it is a habit rather than a paperwork exercise.






Important



When a commit contains work an AI helped with, say so in the commit message. That is the whole rule. You do not have to separate your work from AI-assisted work into different commits, and you do not have to submit transcripts.


This is the convention open-source software development already uses, so you are learning a real practice rather than a classroom one. The canonical form is a trailer line at the end of the message:
Tighten the interpretation of the interaction term

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
A plain sentence in the message body does the same job, and is just as acceptable:
Rewrite the prior justification

Wording tidied up with AI. The choice of prior and the argument for it are mine.
Short messages can simply name it: Fix the join, AI helped debug it or Reformat code with AI. Say what the assistance did where that is not obvious, and be proportionate. A whole section drafted with AI is worth a sentence. A spell check is worth four words.


Why this instead of a chat transcript
A blanket declaration that “generative AI was used to improve the language of this manuscript” cannot be checked by anyone. It is a claim about a process that left no trace. Submitting chat transcripts does not work either, because a transcript cannot be matched to the passages it actually shaped.
Version control solves this, and you are learning it anyway. Your repository already records every change, who made it, when, and exactly what changed. Marking where AI entered turns that ordinary record into the disclosure, produced at the moment the work happens rather than reconstructed weeks later. It is honest about how mixed this work really is, because a sentence you drafted and a model tightened belongs to neither pile, and it rests on the same voluntary integrity that scientific standards have always rested on.
Where the line is. Asking AI to explain a concept, proofread your draft, clean up code you wrote, or help debug an error message: all fine, all encouraged, all easy to attribute. Generating an analysis from scratch and submitting it as your own, or systematically hiding AI involvement so the record shows none: not fine. The common thread is the same in both directions. The history must not misrepresent how the work came about.






Important



You do not need to know any of this yet. Git, commits and commit messages are taught in session 2, and you will practise this convention in every homework from then on. By the time the exam arrives it is a habit rather than a rule to memorise. Nobody is expected to arrive already knowing how to do it.








Note



Two different things, both involving AI. The policy above is about AI you use while doing your own work, which is disclosed in your commit messages. The opt-in feedback described in Section 4 is different: it is run by me, on an explicit license.md opt-in, and it comments on work you have already submitted. Using the feedback pipeline is never something you need to declare.

title: Syllabus
section: The backbone: from research question to empirical answer
text:
The backbone: from research question to empirical answer
Everything in this course builds toward one skill: getting from a question about the world to an answer you can defend, with its uncertainty attached. That route has eight steps, shown in Table 2, and they are the same eight steps every time. The take-home exam is exactly this route, run end to end on a dataset you meet at the end of the term.





Table 2: The 8-step Bayesian workflow. Every homework exercises the steps introduced so far, cumulatively, and the exam runs all eight end to end.










#
Step
What you produce




1
Estimand
The quantity you want to learn about, stated precisely as a target before any model is fitted.


2
Data summary
The data described: measurement, coverage, obvious issues.


3
Formal model
Likelihood and priors written down, the generative model.


4
Prior predictive check
Simulate from the priors, confirm they imply plausible data.


5
Fit
Estimate with brms, weakly-informative priors by default.


6a
MCMC diagnostics
R-hat, ESS, divergences, trace plots. Did sampling work?


6b
Posterior predictive check
Does the fitted model reproduce key features of the data?


7
Interpretation
Answer the estimand on the outcome scale, with uncertainty.


8
Limitations
What the analysis can and cannot support, threats and next steps.







Several of the words in that table probably mean nothing to you yet. That is expected, and it is the honest starting point. Estimand, prior predictive check, R-hat: learning what these are, why each step exists, and what goes wrong when you skip one, is what the term is for. You see the whole route in session 1, before you can walk any of it, so that every later session has somewhere to attach itself. By session 13 you will have run all eight steps yourself, more than once.
The Glossary holds the short version of every term, and each session’s slides hold the long version.

title: Syllabus
text:
Session plan
What each session covers, and what you should be able to do afterwards. Dates, slides, homework and readings are on the Schedule.






Note



This is a preliminary plan and may be revised or updated throughout the semester.



Session 1: Introduction

09 September 2026 · workflow steps 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8

An orientation session. We fill in a short welcome survey together, then work out what statistics is doing at its core: counting, and asking how much a count could have varied by chance. The survey answers become a dataset of our own, and we use it for a first glance at Bayesian inference, running a whole analysis end to end before taking any single step apart. We close on the normal distribution, the one piece of notation that analysis leaned on throughout.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Say what statistics is doing at its core: counting, reasoning about how much a count could have varied by chance, and telling signal from noise.
Tell an estimand, an estimator and an estimate apart, and say what makes a claim an inference.
Get a first glance at Bayesian inference by following a worked analysis of a dataset we collected in the room.
Name the eight steps that analysis followed, which is also the shape of the take-home exam.
Read a normal distribution: what the mean and the standard deviation do to the curve, and where the 68 and 95 percent rule comes from.
Say how the course is structured, and find your way around the course site: schedule, syllabus, glossary and the homework flow.



Session 2: Reproducible literate programming with Quarto and Git

16 September 2026 · Scientific programming fundamentals

The working environment, and the habits that make a result checkable by somebody else. Everything happens in Positron from this session onwards.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Understand how Quarto, R, Git and GitHub fit together.
Create a project under version control and render a Quarto document.
Push your first reproducible document to GitHub, and create your own homework repository from a template, inside the course organisation.
Write a commit message a later reader can follow, which is also where AI assistance gets declared.



Session 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions

23 September 2026 · Scientific programming fundamentals

The language itself, and the small vocabulary everything later is assembled from. Time is spent deliberately on reading errors, because that is the skill that makes independent work possible.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Understand the core concepts: objects, functions and pipes.
Know the main data types R uses to store information.
Know the main data structures R uses to organise information.
Access and explore data using [] and $.
Read an error message and work out what R was actually asked to do.



Session 4: The tidyverse

30 September 2026 · Scientific programming fundamentals · workflow step 2

Getting data into a shape that tools can work with, which is most of the work in most analyses. One small dataset is read from a file, made tidy, transformed, joined and summarised, and the pipeline grows one verb at a time. Step 2 of the workflow, the data summary, starts here.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Use Quarto cell options to control what a rendered document shows.
Tell an R error, a Quarto error and a LaTeX error apart, and know where to look for each.
Install and load packages, and call a function as package::function().
Understand what the tidyverse is, why it exists, and what tidy data means.
Import data with readr and reshape wide data into tidy form with pivot_longer().
Wrangle data with the core dplyr verbs, chained with the native pipe.
Combine two tables with left_join(), and summarise groups with group_by() and summarise().



Session 5: Data visualisation

07 October 2026 · Scientific programming fundamentals · workflow step 2

Moving from a plot that displays data to a figure that makes a point, on top of the reshaping and joining from session 4. We close on probabilities and distributions, which is the bridge into the second block.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Verify a join on messy real data, and handle missing values transparently, understanding the risks of imputation.
Build and customise ggplot2 figures through aesthetics, geoms, scales and themes.
Produce publication-ready tables and embed computed results directly in prose with inline code.
Read a distribution as a statement about how plausible each value is.



Session 6: The logic of Bayesian inference

14 October 2026 · The logic of Bayesian inference · workflow steps 3, 4

The conceptual core of the course, and a deliberate change of gear: the programming gets easier and the thinking gets harder. Probability as a description of uncertainty, and the single rule that combines what you believed beforehand with what you observed.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Articulate the distinction between frequentist and Bayesian interpretations of probability, and explain why each suits different questions.
Explain why parameters are treated as uncertain quantities with distributions.
Name and interpret the three core ingredients: prior, likelihood and posterior.
State Bayes’ theorem in full, identify each term, and explain the role of the normalising constant.
Describe how the posterior changes as the prior changes and as data accumulates.
Apply grid approximation in R to compute and visualise a posterior.



Session 7: Markov chain Monte Carlo

21 October 2026 · The logic of Bayesian inference · workflow steps 4, 5, 6

The computational implementation of everything session 6 established. The emphasis is on reading the diagnostics rather than on deriving the algorithms.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Articulate why grid approximation is intractable for realistic models.
Explain the Monte Carlo idea: approximating integrals by random sampling and counting.
Define a Markov chain and explain what a stationary distribution is.
State the Metropolis acceptance rule and show why the normalising constant cancels.
Explain qualitatively how Hamiltonian Monte Carlo differs from random-walk Metropolis, and why it is more efficient.
Interpret brms output: trace plots, R-hat, effective sample size and posterior distributions.
Understand that convergence cannot be proven, only falsified, and recognise what non-convergence looks like.



Session 8: Bivariate linear regression

04 November 2026 · Applied modelling · workflow steps 1, 3, 4, 5, 6

The first full model, deliberately the simplest one: one outcome, one predictor, and the whole workflow run around it. Every later model extends this one rather than replacing it.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Frame a regression problem as estimand (what we want to know), estimator (the procedure) and estimate (the number we get).
Explain what OLS assumes, and see where the classical and the Bayesian account of the same model meet.
Specify weakly informative priors for regression coefficients and defend them on principled grounds.
Understand brms as sampling from the posterior: an estimator that returns a distribution rather than one number.
Interpret brms output and extract quantities of interest, such as predictions and marginal effects.



Session 9: Multivariate linear regression

11 November 2026 · Applied modelling · workflow steps 1, 7

More than one predictor, and the questions that come with it. A set of controls is a claim about how the world works, not a way of being safe.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Explain omitted variable bias, and use a DAG to classify a control variable as a confounder, a mediator or a collider.
Extend the Bayesian regression model to several predictors and interpret each coefficient as a partial effect.
Handle categorical predictors using dummy variables.
Compare competing models with Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-IC).



Session 10: Interaction terms in linear regression

18 November 2026 · Applied modelling · workflow step 7

Effects that are not the same everywhere. Specification is the easy part, and interpretation is where interactions are usually got wrong, so most of the session goes there.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Specify a multiplicative interaction model and interpret the conditional marginal effect of a predictor as a function of its moderator.
Extract posterior marginal effects separately for each level of the moderator.
Compare an interaction model against the additive model with LOO-IC.
Show a conditional effect in a figure rather than asking a reader to combine coefficients.



Session 11: Modelling binary outcomes: logit and probit

25 November 2026 · Applied modelling · workflow steps 3, 7

Outcomes that are yes or no. Nothing about the engine changes here: we are only swapping the likelihood, and then doing the work of getting back to a scale a reader can use.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Explain why linear models are structurally wrong for binary outcomes, and how a Bernoulli likelihood plus a link function resolves it.
Fit and interpret a Bayesian logistic regression in brms, including priors on the logit scale and predicted probability ribbons.
Say how the probit link differs from the logit, and when the choice matters.
Assess model quality with posterior predictive checks, a confusion matrix, ROC and AUC, and compare models with LOO.



Session 12: Introduction to multilevel models

02 December 2026 · Applied modelling · workflow steps 3, 5, 7

Data with structure: candidates in parties, regions in countries, years in states. A primer and your departure point for later work, and the one session that is not on the take-home exam.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Identify hierarchical data and explain why treating grouped observations as independent understates uncertainty.
Describe the three-point spectrum of complete pooling, no pooling and partial pooling, and say when each is right.
Read the (1 | group) formula in brms and interpret the key output quantities.



Session 13: Beyond the course: applying what you have learned

09 December 2026 · Applied modelling · workflow steps 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8

Synthesis and outlook rather than new methods. We consolidate what you already have and hand you a clean runway into the exam.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Name what you learned across the three blocks, and why the course was built this way.
Read a classical regression table, since most of the literature you will meet reports one.
Use the tooling that makes the code and repository part of the exam grade straightforward.
Know exactly what the exam asks for, how it is graded, and how AI use is declared in it.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Two slogans

To understand computations in R, two slogans are helpful: Everything that exists is an object. Everything that happens is a function call.
John Chambers


Objects are named containers holding information.
Functions are operations that take objects and return new ones.
Pipes chain several function calls into one readable sequence.


This quote is the anchor for the whole session. R has a very consistent grammar once these three ideas land.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Objects: storing information


An object has:

a name, how you refer to it
a value, the information stored
a type, what kind of information it is



# assign with <-
country <- "Germany"
gdp_per_capita <- 54300
is_eu_member <- TRUE

# print by typing the name
country

[1] "Germany"

gdp_per_capita

[1] 54300

is_eu_member

[1] TRUE




Read <- aloud as “gets”: country gets the value “Germany”. Nothing is printed when you assign. You have to call the name to see the value.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Practice: make some objects
Do this now.

Create an object called city holding the name of your home town.
Create an object called year holding the current year.
Print both by typing their names.
Look at the Variables pane in Positron. What do you see?
Now run year <- "twenty twenty-six". What happened to year?
Type City with a capital C. What does R say?



year <- 2026
year <- "twenty twenty-six" # silently overwritten
year

[1] "twenty twenty-six"

City # R is case-sensitive

Error:
! object 'City' not found



Two lessons hide in here. Assigning to an existing name overwrites it without asking. city and City are different names, which gives us our first error message. Do not explain the error yet, we come back to it in ten minutes.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Functions: doing things with objects


A function:

takes one or more inputs, called arguments
does something with them
returns an output

function_name(argument1, argument2)


gdp_values <- c(54300, 43800, 33200)

mean(gdp_values)

[1] 43766.67

nchar(country)

[1] 7

# arguments by position, or by name
round(3.14159, 2)

[1] 3.14

round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14




Point at the parentheses: they are what makes something a function call. Named arguments are easier to read later, so prefer them for anything past the first argument.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Practice: call some functions
Do this now.

Create a vector of three numbers with c(), for example the ages of three people you know.
Compute its mean(), max() and sum().
Round the mean to one decimal place with round(), and name the argument.
Try sqrt(-1). What comes back, and what does R print underneath?



ages <- c(21, 24, 23)
round(mean(ages), digits = 1)

[1] 22.7

sqrt(-1)

Warning in sqrt(-1): NaNs produced


[1] NaN



NaN means “not a number”. The message underneath is a warning, not an error: R did something, but it thinks you should know.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Writing your own function



double_it <- function(x) {
  x * 2
}

double_it(21)

[1] 42

double_it(c(1, 2, 3))

[1] 2 4 6




double_it is the name, assigned with <- like any object.
function(x) declares one argument, called x.
The body between { } says what to do with it.
The last line of the body is the output.



A function is itself an object. Collections of published functions are called packages, and we start using them next week.






Tip


Comments say why, and the prose says the rest. In a Quarto document you can write full sentences between code cells, so keep code comments to a few words.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Practice: write a function
Do this now.

Write a function celsius_to_fahrenheit() that takes a temperature in Celsius and returns it in Fahrenheit. The formula is \(F = C \times 1.8 + 32\).
Test it: 0 degrees should give 32, and 100 degrees should give 212.
Pass it a vector of three temperatures at once. Does it still work?
Stretch: write add_tax(price, rate = 0.19) with a default rate, and call it with and without rate.





celsius_to_fahrenheit <- function(celsius) {
  celsius * 1.8 + 32
}
celsius_to_fahrenheit(c(0, 20, 100))

[1]  32  68 212




add_tax <- function(price, rate = 0.19) {
  price * (1 + rate)
}
add_tax(10)

[1] 11.9

add_tax(10, rate = 0.07)

[1] 10.7

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Getting help
Every function has a documentation page.

?mean
help(round)


Usage shows the arguments and their defaults.
Examples, at the very bottom, is usually the fastest way in.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Errors and warnings
When R cannot do what you asked, it tells you, and it is usually right.

An error stops the code. Nothing was computed.
A warning lets the code finish, but flags something suspicious.


Read an error message in two parts:
Error in round("3.14") : non-numeric argument to mathematical function
         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
         where it broke  what went wrong






Important


Read the message before you change anything. The message says what R was actually asked to do, which is often not what you meant to ask.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
section: Three errors you will meet this week
text:
Three errors you will meet this week



Table 1: The three error messages beginners meet most often, and the usual cause behind each.









Message
What it usually means




object 'x' not found
A typo in a name, wrong capitalisation, or a line you have not run yet.


could not find function "f"
A typo in a function name, or a package that is not loaded.


non-numeric argument to ...
Arithmetic on text, often a number stored as "42".







The first one is by far the most common. Nine times out of ten it is capitalisation or a chunk that was never run.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Practice: break it on purpose
Do this now. Run each line, then read the message aloud to your neighbour: where did it break, and what went wrong?

Mean(c(1, 2, 3))

Error in `Mean()`:
! could not find function "Mean"

gpd_per_capita * 2

Error:
! object 'gpd_per_capita' not found

"42" + 1

Error in `"42" + 1`:
! non-numeric argument to binary operator




Mean is not mean, R is case-sensitive.
gpd is a typo for gdp.
"42" is text that only looks like a number.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Chaining operations
Nested calls are read from the inside out, which is hard:

round(mean(sqrt(gdp_values)), digits = 2)

[1] 208.17



With the pipe |> you read left to right, as “and then”:

gdp_values |> sqrt() |> mean() |> round(digits = 2)

[1] 208.17


The pipe puts the thing on its left into the first argument of the function on its right.

The native pipe arrived in R 4.1. Students will meet %>% from magrittr online, which behaves almost the same. This course uses |> throughout.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Practice: rewrite as a pipe
Do this now. Rewrite this nested call as a pipe, and check that both give the same answer.

temps <- c(12, 18, 25, 31)
round(mean(celsius_to_fahrenheit(temps)), digits = 1)

[1] 70.7




temps |> celsius_to_fahrenheit() |> mean() |> round(digits = 1)

[1] 70.7


Your own functions pipe just like the built-in ones.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
section: What kind of information does R store?
text:
What kind of information does R store?



Table 2: The six kinds of values met in this course. The first four are R’s basic types, and factors and dates are built on top of them.










Type
Description
Example




double
Decimal numbers
3.14, 54300.5


integer
Whole numbers
42L, 2026L


character
Text, also called strings
"Germany", "hello"


logical
True or false
TRUE, FALSE


factor
Categories with fixed levels
"low", "medium", "high"


Date
Calendar dates
2026-09-23






class() tells you which one you have.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Numbers: double and integer

gdp <- 54300.5 # double, the default for numbers
seats <- 736L # integer, the L makes it explicit

class(gdp)

[1] "numeric"

class(seats)

[1] "integer"

is.numeric(seats)

[1] TRUE



For most purposes in this course the difference between integer and double does not matter.
What does matter is knowing whether an object is numeric at all, and is.numeric() answers that.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Text: character

capital <- "Berlin"

nchar(capital)

[1] 6

toupper(capital)

[1] "BERLIN"

paste(capital, "is the capital of", country)

[1] "Berlin is the capital of Germany"



Numbers stored as text are not numbers. This is the "42" + 1 error from before, and as.numeric() is the fix:

as.numeric("42") + 1

[1] 43

text:
True or false: logical



population <- 84000000

population > 50000000

[1] TRUE

population == 84000000

[1] TRUE

!is_eu_member

[1] FALSE


Logicals are the backbone of filtering, which is how we pick out rows of data later today.





Table 3: Comparison and logical operators. Each one returns TRUE or FALSE.





Operator
Meaning
Example




<, <=
less than (or equal)
3 < 5


>, >=
greater than (or equal)
5 >= 5


==
equal to
3 == 3

not equal to

(3 > 1) & (5 > 2)

or

%in%
is contained in
"Spain" %in% c("Spain", "Italy")

= assigns and == compares. Writing if (x = 3) when you mean x == 3 is one of the most common slips in any language.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
section: Categories and dates: factor and Date
text:
Categories and dates: factor and Date


Factors are categories with fixed levels.

regime <- factor(
  c("democracy", "autocracy", "democracy"),
  levels = c("autocracy", "hybrid", "democracy")
)
regime

[1] democracy autocracy democracy
Levels: autocracy hybrid democracy



Dates know about the calendar.

treaty <- as.Date("1957-03-25")
Sys.Date() - treaty

Time difference of 25384 days



R stores these differently from plain text so that it can order, count and do arithmetic with them.

Do not go deep. Factors come back naturally in visualisation in week 5.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
section: From one value to a whole dataset
text:
From one value to a whole dataset




Table 4: The data structures of this course, ordered from a single value to a whole dataset. The first four are the objects of linear algebra, and the notation column is the one this course uses from here on.













Concept
In R
Dimensions
Holds
Notation
Other names




Scalar
a length-1 vector
0
one value
\(x\)
constant, single value


Vector
c()
1
one type
\(\mathbf{x}\)
variable, column, feature, series


Matrix
matrix()
2
one type
\(\mathbf{X}\)
design matrix, 2-D array


Tensor
array()
3 or more
one type
\(\mathcal{X}\)
N-d array, cube


Table
data.frame(), tibble
2
one type per column

dataset, rectangular data, spreadsheet


Record
list()
any, nested
anything

container, dictionary, JSON object








Go row by row, top to bottom: each row adds one dimension. The notation is the course convention, fixed once here. Lowercase italic for a scalar, bold lowercase for a vector, bold uppercase for a matrix, calligraphic for a tensor.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Reading the notation

Bold means more than one number. \(x\) is one value, \(\mathbf{x}\) is a whole column of them.
Uppercase means two dimensions. \(\mathbf{X}\) has rows and columns.
Three or more dimensions is a tensor, written \(\mathcal{X}\). We will rarely need one.
In mathematics these hold numbers only. In R they can hold numbers, text or logicals, but always one type at a time.








Important


R has no scalars. A single value is a vector of length 1, so everything that works on a vector works on one value too.




length(5)

[1] 1




A data frame breaks the one-type rule: every column is a vector with its own type, so a dataset can mix numbers, text and logicals.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Vectors: the building block

countries <- c("Germany", "France", "Italy", "Spain", "Turkey")
population <- c(84, 68, 60, 47, 88) # millions
eu_member <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)

length(countries)

[1] 5

population * 1000000 # works on every element at once

[1] 8.4e+07 6.8e+07 6.0e+07 4.7e+07 8.8e+07



A vector holds one type. Mix types, and R silently converts everything to the most general one:

c(1, 2, "three")

[1] "1"     "2"     "three"

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Practice: vectors
Do this now.

Make a vector temps with the maximum temperature of each of the last five days (guess if you do not know).
How many values does it hold? Use length().
Convert the whole vector to Fahrenheit with your own function from earlier.
Predict first: what does c(1, "two", TRUE) return, and of what class?
Predict first: what does c(1, TRUE, FALSE) return?



c(1, "two", TRUE)

[1] "1"    "two"  "TRUE"

c(1, TRUE, FALSE)

[1] 1 1 0



The second one surprises people: TRUE becomes 1 and FALSE becomes 0. That is exactly why sum() of a logical vector counts the TRUEs, which we use in the last practice.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Matrices and arrays, briefly

matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6



Two dimensions, one type.
The workhorse of linear algebra, and of every regression under the hood.
array() generalises the matrix to three or more dimensions, the tensor \(\mathcal{X}\).


Two minutes maximum. It is here for completeness and so the notation is not abstract.

title: Week 3: R fundamentals: data structures, objects and functions
text:
Data frames: the workhorse



Rectangular: rows and columns.
Each column is a vector, so one type per column.
Different columns can have different types.
Each row is one observation.



eu_data <- data.frame(
  country = countries,
  population = population,
  eu_member = eu_member,
  regime = c(rep("democracy", 4), "hybrid")
)

eu_data

  country population eu_member    regime
1 Germany         84      TRUE democracy
2  France         68      TRUE democracy
3   Italy         60      TRUE democracy
4   Spain         47      TRUE democracy
5  Turkey         88     FALSE    hybrid

nrow(eu_data)

[1] 5

ncol(eu_data)

[1] 4

'data.frame':   5 obs. of  4 variables:

  population = 84000000,

country_info

$name

About you

What name would you prefer us to call you?

In what ways did you learn or come across statistics before?


Go round the room. Nine people, so about a minute each.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
What is statistics?
In a nutshell, you may think of statistics as counting.

Counting values. How many people are 20 years old? How many flips were heads? How many birds were observed?
Counting how much you counted. How many observations do we have?
Official counting. Births, deaths, unemployment, crime.
Counting the ways things could have happened. How much could our count have varied by chance? How many heads would a fair coin give us?



Statistics can be thought of as counting, and as reasoning about counts and their possible variation.


The fourth bullet is the one that carries the rest of the term. Say it slowly.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Why statistics?
Fundamentally, we want to learn about the world using observations. Put differently, we want to learn from data.

Estimand: the quantity we want to learn about (what we want).
Estimator: the procedure by which we learn about it (our method).
Estimate: the result that procedure gives us (what we get).


Inference is using known information to infer something unknown.

Collecting measurements to infer the association between two variables.
Collecting a random sample to infer something about a larger population.
Running randomised experiments to infer a potential outcome.


Estimand, estimator, estimate. Three words they will hear every week.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Fundamental issue in statistics

We want to separate noise from signal.
That is, how certain can we be in our estimate?
Put differently: how certain can we be that an estimated association between two variables is a real world association, rather than the result of random variation during our measurement or data collection?
This is the fundamental challenge and task of quantitative methods in all science.


This is the hinge of the whole course. Everything from week 3 onward is machinery for it.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
A question

Do students become more confident in statistics as they progress through their studies?

You just filled out the survey, which asked, among other things, for your current semester and your confidence in reading statistical results.

Re-render the deck now if the local CSV has arrived. Everything from here on is the room.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 1: Clarify the estimand
What precisely do we want to learn about?

The association between semester of study and reported confidence on a 1 to 10 scale.








Warning


An association is not a causal effect. Nobody was assigned a semester, so we are comparing different people rather than following one person through their degree. Causal identification is a separate course.




Students reach for the causal sentence by reflex. Correct it here, once, hard.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 2: Data summary

Semester as an integer.
Confidence as a number from 1 (not at all confident) to 10 (very confident).





View source
distributions <- model_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(semester, conf_stats),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    variable = case_match(
      variable,
      "semester" ~ "Semester",
      "conf_stats" ~ "Confidence"
    )
  )

ggplot(distributions, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_bar(fill = col_1) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Students", title = "One answer at a time")








Figure 1: How the two answers are spread out. Semester on the left, self-rated confidence on the right, one bar per answer given, as tall as the number of students who gave it.








View source
set.seed(2026)
ggplot(model_df, aes(x = semester, y = conf_stats)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.1, colour = col_1, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 10, by = 2), limits = c(1, 10)) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Semester", y = "Confidence", title = "Both answers at once")








Figure 2: Self-rated confidence against current semester, one point per respondent. Points are nudged slightly so that two people giving the same pair of answers stay visible.






The outcome is (nearly) continuous, which is what justifies a linear model.

Read the semester range out loud. If it is one or two values wide, promise the consequence at step 8. The confidence question was the only optional one, so blank answers are dropped here, and that is a decision worth a sentence in any writeup. Test submissions, marked TEST in the free-text box, were dropped before any of this: 6 of them.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 3: Formal model
Given our approximately continuous outcome, and for the sake of simplicity, we use a bivariate linear model.


Outcome family
\[
\text{Confidence}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma)
\tag{1}\]



How to read the outcome family







Note


Equation 1 in words. We assume the outcome, the reported confidence of student \(i\), to be normally distributed with mean \(\mu_i\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\).




Linear predictor
\[
\mu_i = \alpha + \beta \times \text{Semester}_i
\tag{2}\]


How to read the linear predictor







Note


Equation 2 in words. We model the mean confidence score as a function of the reported semester. \(\alpha\) is the baseline level of reported confidence for a hypothetical semester 0 student, the intercept. \(\beta\) is the average change in reported confidence per unit change in semester, and it is therefore our estimand, the slope. Everything the semester does not account for is the residual spread, which is the \(\sigma\) of Equation 1.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 3: The posterior
\[
P(\alpha, \beta, \sigma \mid \text{Data}) \propto \mathcal{L}(\alpha, \beta, \sigma \mid \text{Data}) \times P(\alpha, \beta, \sigma)
\tag{3}\]


How to read the posterior







Note


Equation 3 in words. The probability of our model parameters (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\sigma\)) given the data we collected, here the confidence and semester answers, is proportional to the likelihood, a function assessing the plausibility of different parameter values given our data, multiplied by the prior distributions of those parameters.





The posterior is a full probability distribution, not a single number.

This equation is the whole course in one line. They meet it again in week 3 and week 7.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 3: The priors
A prior is a probability distribution over a parameter before seeing the data. I chose:

\[
\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(5, 2), \qquad \beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2), \qquad \sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(1)
\tag{4}\]


How to read the prior on the intercept







Note


The prior on \(\alpha\) in words. Before evaluating the observed data, the expected intercept sits in the middle of the outcome scale (5), and with 95 percent probability it is 5 plus or minus about 4. As in Equation 1, the pair in \(\mathcal{N}(5, 2)\) is a mean and a standard deviation, which is also what brms expects.






How to read the prior on the slope







Note


The prior on \(\beta\) in words. My prior expectation is that there is no association, hence a mean of 0, but with 95 percent probability it lies between -4 and +4, which would be very large effects on a 10 point scale.






How to read the prior on the residual spread







Note


The prior on \(\sigma\) in words. Before knowing anything from the data I know the spread must be positive, so a normal distribution will not do. Small spreads are a priori more plausible than large ones.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 3: The priors, drawn


View source
priors_drawn <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    parameter = "alpha: the intercept",
    value = seq(-3, 13, length.out = 200),
    density = dnorm(value, mean = 5, sd = 2)
  ),
  tibble(
    parameter = "beta: the slope",
    value = seq(-8, 8, length.out = 200),
    density = dnorm(value, mean = 0, sd = 2)
  ),
  tibble(
    parameter = "sigma: the spread",
    value = seq(0, 8, length.out = 200),
    density = dexp(value, rate = 1)
  )
)

ggplot(priors_drawn, aes(x = value, y = density)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_3, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free") +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    title = "What I believe before seeing any answer"
  )




Figure 3: The three priors as pictures. Each curve says how plausible I find each value of that parameter before seeing a single answer, which is why the slope curve is centred on zero and the spread curve never reaches below it.

Priors are commitments, not conveniences. Centring beta on zero is the honest starting point, not a trick to get a null.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 4: Prior predictive check
What data would our prior beliefs produce?


View source
set.seed(2026)
n_lines <- 100

# One draw from each prior is one possible world. Each world implies a whole line: the average
# answer it expects at every semester.
prior_lines <- tibble(
  draw = 1:n_lines,
  alpha = rnorm(n_lines, mean = 5, sd = 2),
  beta = rnorm(n_lines, mean = 0, sd = 2)
) |>
  expand_grid(semester = 1:10) |>
  mutate(confidence = alpha + beta * semester)

ggplot(prior_lines, aes(x = semester, y = confidence)) +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 0.5,
    xmax = 10.5,
    ymin = 1,
    ymax = 10,
    fill = col_2,
    alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(group = draw), colour = col_3, alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Semester",
    y = "Confidence",
    title = "Answers our priors consider possible"
  )




Figure 4: One hundred regression lines simulated from the priors alone, before any real answer was used. The shaded band is the 1 to 10 scale the survey actually offers, so every line leaving the band is a world our priors think possible and no student could ever report.

This is the step people skip and the step that catches a bad prior. Point at how far past 10 the lines run, and at how few of them stay inside the band at all. Say that this same picture comes back at step 7, once the data has had its say.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 5: Fit the model


View source
model_priors <- c(
  prior(normal(5, 2), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", coef = "semester"),
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma")
)

fit <- brm(
  conf_stats ~ 0 + Intercept + semester,
  data = model_df,
  family = gaussian(),
  prior = model_priors,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  seed = 2026,
  refresh = 0,
  file = here("website", "slides", "data", "week01-fit"),
  file_refit = "on_change"
)


We will learn in week 7 what is going on here in detail.

In short: we update our prior distributions of the parameters by conditioning on the observed data. Computationally we simulate many different possible lines and rank them by their relative plausibility, and what comes back is a distribution of plausible regression lines.

Run this live and talk over the compile. R writes Stan, Stan writes C++, the compiler builds a sampler specific to this model. That wait is the reason week 7 exists.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 6a: MCMC diagnostics


View source
mcmc_plot(fit, type = "trace") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = chain_cols) +
  theme_pubr()




Figure 5: Trace plots for the three parameters. Four searches started in different places and ended up wandering around the same region, which is what a working computation looks like. A line drifting off on its own would be the warning sign.
We are assessing the simulation algorithm here, and we will learn how in week 7.

Say it twice: this is a statement about the computer, not about whether the model is any good.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 6b: Posterior predictive check


View source
set.seed(2026)
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 50) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Confidence",
    title = "Observed answers against what the model predicts"
  )




Figure 6: Posterior predictive check. The dark line is the confidence we actually observed, the pale lines are datasets the fitted model generates. Where they disagree is where the model is wrong about the world.

How well do the estimated parameters, remember that these are distributions, combined with the predictor, replicate our outcome?
Intuition: a model fits a dataset well if it can recover the outcomes well.


Expect over-smoothing: the model predicts a continuous bell where the data is ten whole numbers. Name that. It is honest and it previews week 11.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 7: Interpretation
Each additional semester is associated with a change of 0.47 scale points of confidence, with a 90 percent credible interval from -0.12 to 1. The posterior puts 91 percent of its mass above zero.


View source
line_cloud <- conditional_effects(fit, spaghetti = TRUE, ndraws = 100)

plot(line_cloud, points = TRUE, plot = FALSE)[[1]] +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Semester",
    y = "Confidence",
    title = "Lines that survive contact with the data"
  )




Figure 7: One hundred regression lines drawn from the posterior, with the observed answers on top. The spread of the lines is the honest summary of how far this data settles the question.

Read the sentence verbatim. Never “proves”, never “there is no effect”, never “significant”.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 7: The estimand itself


View source
mcmc_plot(fit, variable = "b_semester", type = "areas", prob = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_2) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Scale points of confidence per semester",
    y = NULL,
    title = "The posterior for the slope"
  )




Figure 8: The posterior for the slope, which is the estimand named at step 1. The dashed line marks no association at all, and how much of the shape sits to either side of it is the answer to the research question.






Note


An interval is the answer, not a decoration on it. A point estimate with no width attached is a claim the data cannot support.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
Step 8: Limitations

Models are always wrong, but some are useful.
It is always important to reflect on what we can learn and what we cannot learn.


Name the concrete ones out loud rather than putting them on the slide. There are nine of us, which is a class and not a sample of any population. Almost everyone here is in the same semester, and no method fixes that. Nobody was assigned a semester, so this compares people, not one person over time. Self-reported confidence is not skill, and it may even move the other way as you learn how much there is to know. The normal likelihood ignores the scale, which is what steps 4 and 6b both showed.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
The 8-step workflow





Table 1: The 8-step Bayesian workflow. Every homework exercises the steps introduced so far, cumulatively, and the exam runs all eight end to end.










#
Step
What you produce




1
Estimand
The quantity you want to learn about, stated precisely as a target before any model is fitted.


2
Data summary
The data described: measurement, coverage, obvious issues.


3
Formal model
Likelihood and priors written down, the generative model.


4
Prior predictive check
Simulate from the priors, confirm they imply plausible data.


5
Fit
Estimate with brms, weakly-informative priors by default.


6a
MCMC diagnostics
R-hat, ESS, divergences, trace plots. Did sampling work?


6b
Posterior predictive check
Does the fitted model reproduce key features of the data?


7
Interpretation
Answer the estimand on the outcome scale, with uncertainty.


8
Limitations
What the analysis can and cannot support, threats and next steps.








Say it plainly: this table is the exam. Every later week deepens one or two of these steps, and every homework runs the steps introduced so far.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
The normal distribution
Equation 1 said that every answer is normally distributed. That distribution has two knobs, and nothing else.

\(\mu\) is the mean, and moving it slides the whole curve left or right.
\(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, and raising it makes the curve wider and flatter.



View source
normal_curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    curve = "mean 5, sd 1",
    x = seq(-2, 12, by = 0.05),
    density = dnorm(x, 5, 1)
  ),
  tibble(
    curve = "mean 5, sd 2",
    x = seq(-2, 12, by = 0.05),
    density = dnorm(x, 5, 2)
  ),
  tibble(
    curve = "mean 8, sd 1",
    x = seq(-2, 12, by = 0.05),
    density = dnorm(x, 8, 1)
  )
)

ggplot(normal_curves, aes(x = x, y = density, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_1, col_3, col_2)) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Two knobs, three curves"
  )




Figure 9: Three normal distributions. Changing the mean slides the curve sideways, changing the standard deviation changes how wide it is, and no other shape is available.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
The 68 and 95 rule
The area under the curve is probability, and for a normal distribution that area always splits the same way, whatever \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) happen to be.


View source
normal_area <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 13, by = 0.05), density = dnorm(x, 5, 2))

ggplot(normal_area, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(normal_area, x >= 1, x <= 9),
    fill = col_1,
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(normal_area, x >= 3, x <= 7),
    fill = col_1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = col_1, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9)) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Density", title = "68 percent inside, then 95 percent")




Figure 10: A normal distribution with mean 5 and standard deviation 2. About 68 percent of the area lies within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95 percent within two, which is where the reading of the prior on the intercept came from.
This is exactly why \(\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(5, 2)\) was read as 5 plus or minus about 4.

title: Week 1: Introduction
text:
The standard normal
\(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, is the reference curve. Every other normal distribution is that same shape, shifted and stretched.
\[
z_i = \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma}
\tag{5}\]


View source
standard_normal <- tibble(z = seq(-3.5, 3.5, by = 0.05), density = dnorm(z))

ggplot(standard_normal, aes(x = z, y = density)) +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(standard_normal, z >= -2, z <= 2),
    fill = col_1,
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(standard_normal, z >= -1, z <= 1),
    fill = col_1,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = col_1, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3) +
  theme_pubr() +
  labs(
    x = "z, standard deviations from the mean",
    y = "Density",
    title = "The reference curve"
  )




Figure 11: The standard normal, mean 0 and standard deviation 1, shaded the same way as Figure 10. The axis is no longer scale points but standard deviations, and the dashed line marks z equal to 2, the edge of the 95 percent region.
Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation turns any normal variable into a standard normal one, which is the curve in Figure 11. A value of \(z_i = 2\) then means the same thing everywhere: two standard deviations above the mean, which Figure 10 puts at the edge of the 95 percent region.

Do not derive anything. The point is only that a standard deviation is a unit of distance.
