title: Quantitative Methods in IR/EU Politics: Learning from data
text:
What this course is
An introduction to quantitative methods for international relations and European politics, taught with free and open source state of the art tools: R, Quarto, Git and GitHub, all inside Positron. You will learn regression as a way of describing relationships in data, and Bayesian inference as a way of saying how certain you are about them.
The whole term runs toward one skill, an eight-step analysis taking you from a research question to an empirical answer with its uncertainty attached. You see that route in session 1, deepen one part of it each week, and run it end to end yourself in the take-home exam. No programming experience and no statistics beyond descriptives are assumed.

title: Quantitative Methods in IR/EU Politics: Learning from data
text:
Where to go next

Syllabus for the full details: objectives, logistics, grading, the exam, the policies, and what each session covers.
Schedule for dates, slides, homework and sample solutions.
Installation guide for the software. Work through it before the first session, so problems are easy to fix together rather than urgent.
Glossary for the terminology, which arrives quickly in a course like this.

title: Glossary
text:
The vocabulary of the course, collected in one place and sorted alphabetically. Every entry is tagged with the week in which you first meet it, and with that week’s block, so you can still read this page in the same order as the Schedule if you want to. Terms inside a definition link to their own entries, and software entries link to their official documentation. The page grows with the course: a term is added in the week it is taught.
Nothing here replaces the slides. A glossary entry is the short version you can check quickly, not the explanation.

title: Glossary
text:
A

Array and tensor

The generalisation of a matrix to three or more dimensions, created in R with array(). In mathematics it is called a tensor and written in calligraphic as \(\mathcal{X}\), and this course rarely needs one.
Documentation: R documentation: arrays
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Assignment

Storing a value in an object under a name with <-, read aloud as “gets”: country <- "Germany". Assigning to a name that already exists overwrites it without asking.
Documentation: R documentation: assignment operators
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

title: Glossary
text:
B

Base R

The functions R ships with before any package is installed, such as mean(), round() and data.frame(). Everything in week 3 was base R.
Documentation: R documentation: the base package
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r

title: Glossary
text:
C

Caption

The descriptive text attached to a figure or a table, written in the Markdown or set with the fig-cap and tbl-cap cell options. A good caption lets a reader understand the figure or table without the surrounding text.
Documentation: Quarto: figures
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

Case sensitivity

R treats upper and lower case as different, so city and City are two different names and Mean() is not mean(). A wrong capital letter is the most common cause of an “object not found” error.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Cell option

A #| line at the top of a code cell that controls it, such as label:, echo: false (hide the code), eval: false (do not run it), include: false (show nothing) or error: true (show the error and keep rendering). Set under execute: in the YAML header, an option applies to every cell instead.
Documentation: Quarto: execution options
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

Character

R’s type for text, also called a string, always written in quotes: "Germany". A number in quotes is text, so "42" + 1 is an error until it is converted.
Documentation: R documentation: character vectors
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Clone

Making a local copy of a remote repository, including its full history. It is how a homework repository gets from GitHub onto your computer.
Documentation: Git: git clone
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Code cell

A block of executable code inside a .qmd, also called a code chunk, which starts with three backticks and {r} and ends with three backticks. Quarto runs it on render and places the result directly underneath, and every cell in this course carries a label.
See also: Cell option, Inline code.
Documentation: Quarto: computations
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto r

Codebook

The documentation of a dataset, listing every variable with what it measures, its scale or categories, and how missing values are coded. Read it before analysing, because column names rarely say enough.
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

Coercion

R changing values from one type to another automatically, most often when a vector mixes types, without anyone asking for it. c(1, 2, "three") becomes all text and c(1, TRUE, FALSE) becomes the numbers 1, 1 and 0, whereas type conversion is the same change made on purpose.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Column type

The data type of a column, shown in short form when a tibble is printed: <chr> character, <dbl> double, <int> integer, <lgl> logical, <fct> factor and <date> date. Check it first with new data, because a number or a date read in as text breaks everything that follows.
Documentation: tibble: column types
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Comment

Text after a # on a line of code, which R ignores when it runs the code. In a Quarto document the prose carries the reasoning, so comments stay short and say why a line is there.
Documentation: R Language Definition: comments
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Commit

One recorded snapshot of the project: the staged changes, who made them, when, and a message saying what changed. A commit is the unit of history, so it should be a meaningful checkpoint.
See also: Commit history.
Documentation: Git: git commit
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Commit history

The list of all commits in a repository, newest first, each with its message, author and date, shown by git log or in Positron’s Source Control view. It is the record of how the project developed, and the way back to any earlier version.
Documentation: Pro Git: viewing the commit history
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Commit message

The short text attached to a commit, written for a future reader, most importantly future you. “Add figure and cross-reference to introduction” helps, “Update” does not, and it is also where AI assistance gets declared.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git workflow

Comparison and logical operators

Operators that return TRUE or FALSE: <, >, ==, !=, %in%, combined with & (and), | (or) and ! (not). Note that = assigns and == compares.
Documentation: R documentation: relational operators
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Console

The interactive R session in Positron, where code runs line by line and prints its result straight away. Use it to try things out and for one-off commands such as install.packages(), and keep everything that belongs to the analysis in the document.
See also: Fresh R session.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals r workflow

CRAN

The Comprehensive R Archive Network, a network of servers around the world that store identical, up-to-date versions of R and of more than 20,000 contributed packages. install.packages() downloads from it.
Documentation: CRAN
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Cross-reference

A numbered, clickable reference from the text to a labelled figure, table, equation or section, written as @fig-example. A label survives reordering, and a phrase such as “the figure below” does not.
Documentation: Quarto: cross-references
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

CSV

Comma-separated values: a plain-text file with one row per line and the columns separated by commas, which any program can read. Files saved by a German-language Excel often separate columns with semicolons instead, and readr reads those with read_csv2().
Documentation: readr
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

title: Glossary
text:
D

Data cycle

The stages of a data analysis: import the data, tidy it, transform it, visualise it, model it, and communicate the result. In a real project the middle stages loop, because a plot or a model often sends you back to tidy or transform again.
Documentation: R for Data Science: introduction
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow data

Data frame and tibble

R’s structure for a rectangular dataset: a table in which each column is a vector with its own type, so one dataset can mix numbers, text and logicals. A tibble is the tidyverse’s modern reimagining of the data frame, with friendlier printing and fewer surprises.
See also: Tidy data, Column type.
Documentation: R documentation: data frames
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals data r

Data structure

How R organises values: from a single value, through vectors, matrices and arrays, to data frames and lists. Each step adds a dimension or, for data frames and lists, the freedom to mix types.
See also: Scalar, Vector, Matrix, Array and tensor, Data frame and tibble, List.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Data summary

Step 2 of the eight-step workflow: describing the data an analysis uses, its variables, measurement, coverage and obvious issues, before any model. In practice it is a pipeline ending in a captioned table, and every decision that changes the data, such as dropping missing values, is named in the text.
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow data

Data type

What kind of information a value is: double, integer, character or logical, plus factor and Date built on top of them. class() tells you which one you have.
See also: Double and integer, Character, Logical, Factor, Date, Column type.
Documentation: R Language Definition: basic types
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Date

R’s type for calendar dates, created from text in the form year-month-day, as in as.Date("1957-03-25"). A date knows about the calendar, so dates can be sorted and subtracted.
Documentation: R documentation: dates
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Default argument value

The value an argument takes when the call does not supply one, set in the function definition, as digits = 0 is for round(). It is why many functions work with a single argument, and the Usage section of a help page lists every default.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Diff

A comparison of two versions of a file, showing what was removed, what was added and where. Reading the diff before you commit is how you check that a commit contains what you think it does.
Documentation: Git: git diff
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Double and integer

R’s two numeric types: double for decimal numbers, the default, and integer for whole numbers, written with an L as in 42L. The difference rarely matters here, but whether a value is numeric at all does, and is.numeric() answers that.
Documentation: R documentation: numeric vectors
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

title: Glossary
text:
E

Eight-step workflow

The fixed sequence every analysis in this course follows, from stating the estimand to reflecting on limitations. It is also the shape of the take-home exam, and each week deepens one or two of its steps, starting with the data summary.
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow

Error and warning

An error stops the code and nothing is computed, while a warning lets the code finish but flags something suspicious. Read an error in two parts, where it broke and what went wrong, before you change anything.
See also: Render layers.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Estimand

The quantity we want to learn about from data, such as the association between two variables, stated precisely before any analysis. Naming it first is what keeps the estimator and the estimate answerable to a question.
Week 1 Orientation workflow interpretation

Estimate

The output of the estimator: the result we get back once the method has been applied to the data. Ideally it corresponds to the estimand, and checking how far it does is part of every analysis.
Week 1 Orientation interpretation

Estimator

The procedure, our method, that turns data into an estimate of the estimand. The same estimand can be approached with different estimators, so the choice is one you have to justify.
Week 1 Orientation workflow model

Excel workbook and sheet

An Excel file (.xlsx or .xls) is a workbook that can hold several sheets, each its own table. The readxl package, installed with the tidyverse but not loaded by it, lists the sheets and reads one at a time.
Documentation: readxl
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

title: Glossary
text:
F

Factor

R’s type for categories, a vector encoded with a fixed set of levels, such as autocracy, hybrid and democracy. Stored this way, categories can be ordered and counted, and the order of the levels controls how they appear in tables and plots.
Documentation: R documentation: factors
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

File extension

The ending of a file name, such as .csv, .xlsx, .dta or .qmd, which tells you and your software what format the file is in. Each data format has its own reading function, so the extension tells you which one to reach for.
Documentation: R for Data Science: data import
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

Fresh R session

An R session with nothing in it yet, which is what Quarto starts for every render before running every cell from top to bottom. An object you created only in the console does not exist there, which is the usual reason a render fails with “object not found” while the console works.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r quarto

Function and argument

A function is a named, reusable piece of code that takes inputs, its arguments, and returns an output, called as name(argument1, argument2). Arguments can be given by position or by name, and naming them makes code readable a month later.
See also: Default argument value, Writing a function, Help page.
Documentation: An Introduction to R: named arguments and defaults
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

title: Glossary
text:
G

Git

A free and open-source distributed version control system that records the history of a project as a series of commits. It answers what changed, when, and why, and it lets you go back.
Documentation: Pro Git: what is Git?
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

GitHub

A cloud-based platform where you can store, share and work together with others on Git repositories. Git is the version control system on your computer, and GitHub is the service that hosts the remote copy, which is how homework is distributed and submitted in this course.
Documentation: GitHub Docs: about GitHub and Git
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Grouped summary

Reducing a table to summary statistics, such as a count or a mean, once for each group defined by the values of one or more columns. In dplyr, group_by() sets the groups without changing anything you can see, summarise() then returns one row per group, and count() is the shortcut for the number of rows per group.
Documentation: dplyr: grouped data
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data r

title: Glossary
text:
H

Help page

The documentation every R function has, opened with ?mean or help(mean). Its sections say what the function does, which arguments it takes and their defaults (Usage and Arguments) and what it returns (Value), and the Examples at the bottom are usually the fastest way in.
Documentation: An Introduction to R: getting help
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

title: Glossary
text:
I

Indexing

Picking values out of a structure: [ ] by position or by condition, and $ by name, for data frames and lists. On a data frame [row, column] takes both (a blank means all), a negative position drops instead of keeps, and a logical vector keeps the elements where it is TRUE, which is filtering.
Documentation: R documentation: extract or replace parts of an object
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Inference

Learning from data: using what we have observed to say something about what we have not. Measuring two variables to learn about their association, or sampling people to learn about a population, are both inference.
See also: Estimand, Signal and noise.
Week 1 Orientation probability interpretation

Inline code

R code inside a sentence, written as a backtick, the letter r, a space, the code and a closing backtick, whose result replaces it in the rendered text. A number reported this way updates itself when the data or the code changes.
Documentation: Quarto: inline code
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto r

title: Glossary
text:
J

Join

Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key, so the result has the columns of both. The four joins differ only in which rows survive when a key has no partner: a left join keeps every row of the first table, a right join every row of the second, an inner join only the matches, and a full join everything.
Documentation: dplyr: mutating joins
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

title: Glossary
text:
K

Key

The column, or columns, a join matches rows on, such as country, and when it has a different name in each table, join_by() says which columns belong together. A key matches text exactly, so one spelling difference silently produces NA: count the missing values after every join.
Documentation: dplyr: join specifications
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

title: Glossary
text:
L

Label

A unique name given to a figure, table, section or code cell, such as #fig-map, #tbl-results or #sec-intro, whose prefix says what kind of thing it is. A label is what a cross-reference points to.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

LaTeX

A high-quality typesetting system, the last layer of a PDF render, which turns the converted document into the PDF. Its errors usually come from a special character in your prose, such as %, &, $ or a stray backslash.
Documentation: The LaTeX Project
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

List

R’s flexible container, created with list(), which can hold anything, including other lists. You will rarely build one yourself, but every fitted model in this course comes back as one.
Documentation: R documentation: lists
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Literate programming

Writing code, the prose that explains it and its results in a single document, so the reasoning and the computation cannot drift apart. Quarto is the tool we use for it.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow quarto

Local repository

The copy of a repository on your own computer, where you edit files and make commits. Your commits live only here until you push them to the remote.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Logical

R’s type for true or false, TRUE and FALSE, which every comparison returns. Logicals are the backbone of filtering, and the sum of a logical vector counts its TRUE values.
Documentation: R documentation: logical vectors
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

title: Glossary
text:
M

Markdown

The plain-text formatting syntax used in the body of a .qmd: *italics*, **bold**, # for headings, > for a block quote, - for a list item, [text](url) for a link and | pipes for a table. Quarto uses Pandoc’s flavour of Markdown, which stays readable as source and still renders to a formatted document.
Documentation: Quarto: Markdown basics
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

Masking

What happens when a loaded package has a function with the same name as one already available, so the newer one wins. library(tidyverse) reports, for example, that dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter(), and the namespace operator :: picks one explicitly.
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Matrix

A two-dimensional arrangement of values of one type, in rows and columns, created with matrix() and written in bold uppercase as \(\mathbf{X}\). It is the workhorse of linear algebra, and of every regression under the hood.
Documentation: R documentation: matrices
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Mean and standard deviation

The mean \(\mu\) is the centre of a distribution, and moving it slides a normal curve left or right. The standard deviation \(\sigma\) is its spread, and raising it makes the curve wider and flatter.
Week 1 Orientation probability data

Median

The middle value of a set of numbers once they are sorted, so half the values lie below it and half above. Unlike the mean, it barely moves when a few values are extreme, which makes it the better summary of skewed data such as income.
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals probability data

Missing values in calculations

Most summary functions, such as mean() or sum(), return NA if any value is missing, because the true answer is then unknown. Their argument na.rm = TRUE removes the missing values first, which is a decision about your data worth stating in the text.
Documentation: R documentation: mean
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

title: Glossary
text:
N

NA

R’s marker for a missing value, “not available”. It appears when a value was never recorded, when a conversion fails and when a join finds no match, so always check how many you have.
See also: Missing values in calculations.
Documentation: R documentation: NA
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Namespace (::)

Calling a function by naming the package it lives in, written package::function(), as in readxl::read_excel(). It makes the source clear, needs no library() for a one-off call, and settles which function you mean when two packages share a name.
See also: Masking.
Documentation: R documentation: double colon
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r

NaN

R’s value for “not a number”, the result of a calculation with no defined answer, such as 0 / 0 or sqrt(-1). It usually comes with a warning, and R also counts it as a missing value.
Documentation: R documentation: finite, infinite and NaN numbers
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Native pipe

The |> operator, which passes the value on its left into the function call on its right as the first argument, so a sequence of steps reads left to right, as “and then”. This course uses |> throughout and not the older %>% from the magrittr package.
See also: Pipeline.
Documentation: R documentation: forward pipe operator
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Nested function call

A function call inside another, such as round(mean(x), digits = 1), which R evaluates from the inside out. Deep nesting is hard to read, which is what the native pipe is for.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Normal distribution

The symmetric bell-shaped distribution, written \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)\) in this course. It has exactly two knobs, the mean and the standard deviation, and no other shape is available.
See also: Rule of 68 and 95 percent, Standard normal distribution.
Week 1 Orientation probability

title: Glossary
text:
O

Object

A named container holding information, with a name, a value and a type. In R, everything that exists is an object, including functions and fitted models.
Documentation: R Language Definition: objects
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Observation

One unit of what was measured, such as one country in one year. In tidy data each observation has its own row.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals data

One sentence per line

Writing prose in a .qmd with each sentence on its own source line. The rendered document looks the same, but the diff can now show a change sentence by sentence.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto git

Open-source licence

A licence that allows anyone to use, copy, change and share a piece of work under stated conditions, such as keeping the copyright notice, the MIT License being a short and common example. Adding it as license.md to a homework repo is how you opt in to AI feedback.
Documentation: GitHub Docs: licensing a repository
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow git

Opt-in AI feedback

The only individual feedback on homework: if your submission repo contains an open-source licence as license.md, an AI compares your work with the sample solution and adds a FEEDBACK.pdf to your repo. Without that file your submission is not processed at all.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow

Output format

The kind of document a render produces, such as HTML, PDF or Word, set with format: in the YAML header. The source stays the same whatever the format: one source, several outputs.
Documentation: Quarto: all formats
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

title: Glossary
text:
P

Package

A bundle of R functions, their documentation and sometimes data, that someone wrote and shared, whose contents become available only once it is loaded. Install it once with install.packages() in the console, and load it every session with library() at the top of the document.
See also: CRAN, Namespace (::).
Documentation: An Introduction to R: packages
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Pandoc

A universal document converter, which Quarto runs after the code cells have executed to turn Markdown into HTML, Word or LaTeX. An error from the YAML header surfaces at this layer, with a line and column number.
Documentation: Pandoc
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

Pipeline

A sequence of steps chained with the native pipe, each taking the previous result, from reading a file to a finished table. Pipelines are powerful, so build them one step at a time and check the result at every step.
Documentation: R for Data Science: data transformation
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r workflow

Positron

A free data science environment, an IDE (integrated development environment), for R and Python, and the editor this course works in. By default the editor sits above the console and the terminal, with the Variables and Plots panes on the right and views such as the Explorer and Source Control in the Activity Bar.
Documentation: Positron: layout
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow

Probability density

The height of the curve of a continuous probability distribution. The density itself is not a probability: the area under the curve between two values is.
Week 1 Orientation probability

Probability distribution

A description of how plausible each possible value of a quantity is. For a continuous quantity it is drawn as a density curve, and the area under the curve between two values is the probability of landing between them.
Week 1 Orientation probability

Project root

The top folder of a project, the fixed point every other path is expressed relative to. The here package builds every path from it, as in here("data", "file.csv"), which is what makes a project run on a machine other than yours.
Documentation: here package
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow r

Push and pull

Sending your local commits to the remote (push), and bringing commits from it into your local repository (pull). The Sync button in Positron does both.
Documentation: Git: git push
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

title: Glossary
text:
Q

Quarto

An open-source scientific and technical publishing system that turns a .qmd file of Markdown and executable code cells into HTML, PDF, Word, slides and more. Everything in this course, including this page, is a Quarto document.
Documentation: Quarto: Hello, Quarto (Positron)
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

title: Glossary
text:
R

Remote

A version of your repository hosted on the internet, normally on GitHub, that you push to and pull from. The remote is what makes the work shared rather than local.
Documentation: Pro Git: working with remotes
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Render

Quarto’s term for taking a source .qmd, running its code cells and producing a new output document, from the Preview button in Positron or with quarto render in the terminal. A submission that does not render is not a submission, because nobody else can reproduce it.
See also: Fresh R session, Render layers.
Documentation: Quarto: rendering
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto workflow

Render layers

The programs a PDF render passes through in turn: R runs the code cells, Pandoc converts the Markdown, and LaTeX typesets the PDF. An error message shows which layer failed, and only the first error counts, so fix that one and render again.
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals quarto

Repository

A project under version control: its files together with the full history of every change, usually shortened to “repo”. You get one either by initialising a folder as a new repository, which is what git init and Positron’s Source Control pane do, or by cloning an existing one.
See also: Local repository, Remote.
Documentation: Pro Git: getting a Git repository
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Reproducible research

Research whose results can be regenerated from the raw data and the code alone, by someone else, on another machine. The practical test is whether one render rebuilds every number and figure in the output.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow

Reshaping

Changing the layout of a table without changing its information, in the tidyverse by pivoting: pivot_longer() turns column names into values of a new variable, and pivot_wider() turns values back into column names. Keep working data long and tidy, and pivot wider only for a table meant for a reader.
Documentation: tidyr: pivoting
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data r

Rule of 68 and 95 percent

For any normal distribution, about 68 percent of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95 percent within two. It is why \(\mathcal{N}(5, 2)\) reads as “5, plus or minus about 4”.
Week 1 Orientation probability

title: Glossary
text:
S

Sample solution

A complete worked answer to a homework, published for everyone after the due date. Comparing it with your own submission is the default way to get feedback in this course.
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals workflow

Scalar

A single value, written in italic lowercase as \(x\) in this course. R has no scalars: a single value is a vector of length 1, so everything that works on a vector works on one value too.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Scientific notation

Writing a very large or very small number as a number times a power of ten, where e means “times ten to the”: 1e6 is a million and 2.5e-3 is 0.0025. R prints large numbers this way too, so 8.4e+07 is 84 million.
Documentation: R documentation: numeric constants
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Signal and noise

Signal is the real pattern in the world that we want to learn about, and noise is random variation from measurement or data collection. Telling the two apart, and saying how certain we can be that we have, is the fundamental task of learning from data.
Week 1 Orientation probability interpretation

Source Control pane

The view in Positron’s Activity Bar that shows your changed files and lets you stage and commit them with a few clicks. It is Positron’s built-in interface to Git, so everything it does can also be done with Git commands in the terminal.
Documentation: Positron: Git
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git workflow

Stage

Marking changes to go into the next commit, with git add or the plus button in the Source Control pane. Staging lets you commit some changes and keep others back, so each commit stays one meaningful step.
Documentation: Pro Git: recording changes
Week 2 Scientific programming fundamentals git

Standard normal distribution

The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). Every other normal distribution is that same shape, shifted and stretched, which is what standardising undoes.
Week 1 Orientation probability

Standardising

Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, \(z_i = (x_i - \mu) / \sigma\), which turns any normal variable into a standard normal one. A value of \(z_i = 2\) then means the same thing everywhere: two standard deviations above the mean.

Table of contents

Terminal

A text interface to your computer’s operating system, where you type commands such as ls (list files), cd (change directory, cd .. for one folder up) and clear. It is not the console: the terminal runs system commands such as quarto render, and the console runs R.

Tidy data

Data in which every column is a variable, every row is an observation, and every cell holds a single value. Most tools assume this shape, and most of the work of an analysis is getting data into it.
See also: Wide and long format, Reshaping.
Documentation: tidyr: tidy data
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals data

Tidyverse

An opinionated collection of R packages designed for data science, which share an underlying design philosophy, grammar and data structures. library(tidyverse) loads the core packages, among them readr for reading files, tidyr for reshaping, dplyr for transforming with verbs and ggplot2 for plots.
See also: Tidy data, Data cycle.
Documentation: tidyverse: packages
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Type conversion

Deliberately changing a value from one type to another with an as. function, such as as.numeric("42") or as.character(2026). A value that cannot be converted, such as as.numeric("five"), becomes NA with a warning.

title: Glossary
text:
V

Variable

One characteristic measured across observations, such as population or regime type. In tidy data each variable has its own column.
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals data

Variables pane

The Positron pane that lists every object in your current R session, with its type and a preview of its value. It shows what exists in the console, which can differ from what exists in a fresh R session.
Documentation: Positron: Variables pane
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r workflow

Vector

An ordered set of values of one type, created with c() and written in bold lowercase as \(\mathbf{x}\). It is the building block of R, and arithmetic on a vector works on every element at once.
See also: Vectorisation, Coercion.
Documentation: R documentation: vectors
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Vectorisation

Applying an operation to every element of a vector at once, without writing a loop: c(84, 68) * 1000000 multiplies both values. Most R operators and functions are vectorised, which is why a function written for one value usually works on a whole column too.
Documentation: An Introduction to R: vector arithmetic
Week 3 Scientific programming fundamentals r

Verb

A tidyverse function named for what it does to a table, such as dplyr’s filter() (keep rows), select() (keep columns), mutate() (create or change columns) and arrange() (sort rows). Every verb takes a table first, names columns without quotes, and returns a new table, so verbs chain into a pipeline.
Documentation: dplyr: introduction
Week 4 Scientific programming fundamentals r data

Version control

A system that records changes to a file or set of files over time, so that you can recall specific versions later. Git is the version control system this course uses.

Wide and long format

Wide data spreads one variable across several columns, for example one column per year, and long data stacks it into one column with a second column saying which year. Going from one to the other is reshaping.

Working directory

The folder the terminal or R currently treats as “here” when it resolves a relative path. It changes depending on how code is run, which is why paths in this course are built from the project root instead.

Writing a function

Creating your own function with function() and assigning it to a name like any object: double_it <- function(x) { x * 2 }. The arguments go between the parentheses, the body between the braces, and the value of the last line of the body is the output.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Why so many tools?
This course introduces a range of software tools which, taken together, form a powerful and contemporary toolbox for transparent, reproducible and scalable empirical research. Rather than relying on a single piece of software, you will learn how different tools interact and complement one another, much as they do in real research workflows.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Feeling overwhelmed is normal
Meeting many tools at once can feel complex and, at times, overwhelming. That is entirely normal and an expected part of the learning process. Research environments evolve quickly, with new libraries, platforms and technologies (including AI-based ones) constantly emerging. So one of the central goals here is not just to teach specific tools, but to help you learn how to learn programming and computational methods, which is an essential and transferable skill for any data-driven career.

title: Getting started: installation guide
section: Tools as part of a research workflow
text:
Tools as part of a research workflow
These tools are not only for performing calculations or producing results. They also help you document decisions, record analytical steps, collaborate with others, and build workflows that can be extended, reproduced and scaled. In that sense the course aims to familiarise you with research practices that resemble how high-quality empirical work is actually done.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Learning concepts, not just commands
Given the scope of the course, we will only scratch the surface, the tip of the iceberg, of many of these tools. I will emphasise conceptual understanding instead: how the tools work in principle, why they are useful, and when they help. That foundation is what lets you work independently and confidently with these tools, and with future ones, beyond the course.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Pragmatism over dogmatism
The workflow and software stack presented here reflect my own experience and day-to-day research practice. They are not meant to be prescriptive or dogmatic. There is no single correct way to code or to structure an analysis, and many different approaches reach the same goal. Pragmatism matters, so tools should serve your research questions and not the other way around.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Installation timeline
This page lists all the software you are expected to install. Not every tool is used in the first week, but install everything as early as you can. That gives us time to troubleshoot, and it keeps technical setup from becoming a bottleneck once we move into substantive work.






Tip



Do the steps in the order given. R comes before Positron, and the C++ compiler comes before brms. Each step assumes the ones above it are done.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
What the words mean
The instructions below say things like “run this in the Console” and “open a Terminal”. Those are two different places, and mixing them up is the single most common reason a step appears not to work. Figure 1 shows where each of them lives once Positron is installed.






Figure 1: The Positron interface. The Editor in the middle is where your .qmd and .R files are open. The Console (bottom) is where you type R commands and see their results. The Terminal sits next to the Console and is where you talk to your operating system rather than to R. Panes can be moved around, so yours may not look identical, but the names stay the same.



Console. An R session waiting for R commands. If an instruction shows R code, such as install.packages("here"), it goes here. You can tell it is an R console by the > prompt at the start of the line.
Terminal. A place to type commands to your operating system, not to R. On Windows this is PowerShell, on macOS it is the Terminal app, and Positron has one built in. Commands such as git --version or quarto install tinytex go here, and running them in the Console instead will produce an error.
Editor. The main pane where files are open for editing. Writing code in the Editor and then running it is the normal way to work, because the Editor keeps a record and the Console does not.
Pane. One of the rectangular regions of the window. Positron lets you show, hide and rearrange them, which is worth doing once you know what each is for.






Note



A quick way to tell them apart. If the line starts with > you are in the R Console. If it starts with your username, a folder name, or PS C:\>, you are in a Terminal.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Why Positron and not RStudio?
If you have had any contact with R already, or know people who have, you may know that one of the most widespread IDEs for R is RStudio. I decided to teach Positron for a few reasons.

It is a modern and genuinely useful IDE for both programming and project management, with features that integrate coding in R and writing in Quarto well.
It works neatly with R and Python. Although we learn R here, being able to add Python later is valuable, as many other scientific disciplines and private enterprises use Python.
It has very good graphical integration of version control with Git.
It is built on an open-source predecessor of VS Code, one of the most popular editors globally, so it is very similar to it.
If you learn to work with Positron, you will have no problem adapting to RStudio.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Install the toolchain
Pick your operating system once, below. The tab you choose stays selected for the whole guide, so work straight down it from step 1 to step 8.

WindowsmacOS



1. Install R
R is a free and open-source programming language widely used for statistical analysis, data visualisation and reproducible research. R is our main tool, and you can think of it as the engine that does our calculations.1

Go to the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) website.
Click “Download R for Windows”.
Select base and download the installation file.
Run the downloaded file to install R.







Note



Take the current release rather than a specific version number. CRAN always offers the latest release at the top of the download page, and that is the one to take. Note which version you installed, because Rtools in step 3 has to match it.




2. Install Positron
Positron is our integrated development environment (IDE), the program you actually sit in front of to write R. If R is the engine, Positron is the dashboard: it gives you a graphical interface to control, monitor and run R code. It is a free, source-available IDE designed specifically for data science with R and Python.

Navigate to https://positron.posit.co/install.html.
Install all prerequisites listed for Windows. You can ignore the Python setup and R setup panes.
Accept the license agreement by ticking the box.
Click Download Positron for Windows and run the downloaded file.

Once it opens, find the Console and the Terminal described in Section 7.


3. Install a C++ compiler (Rtools)
Some R packages we use later rely internally on C++, a much more efficient language for computationally intensive tasks. For this to work, R needs access to a C++ compiler so it can compile and run C++ code behind the scenes. You will not usually interact with C++ directly, but the compiler is required to install and use certain packages, brms among them.

Go to the Rtools page on CRAN.
Download and install the Rtools version that matches the R version you installed in step 1. The page lists one Rtools release per R release, so R 4.5.x takes Rtools45.
Follow the installation instructions and keep the default settings unless told otherwise.







Warning



A mismatched Rtools version is the most common setup failure on Windows. If brms later fails to install with a compilation error, check the Rtools version against your R version first. Installing a newer R afterwards means installing the matching Rtools too.




4. Install Git
Git is a free and open-source version control system, a tool that tracks changes in your files over time. It lets you see what changed, revert to earlier versions, and collaborate without overwriting other people’s work. GitHub is an online platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features such as pull requests, issues and automated workflows. Together they make it easier to write code, analyse data, and manage research projects transparently and reproducibly.

Go to the Git download page.
Press the Click here to download link.
Open the downloaded .exe file and follow the installation instructions.
Open a Terminal (PowerShell, or the Terminal pane in Positron) and type:

git --version
You should see a version number. If so, Git is installed correctly.


5. Configure Git
To use Git you need to set a name and an email address. These are attached to every change (commit) you make, acting like a digital signature. You do not have to use your full name, but it is recommended. Run both lines in the Terminal, substituting your own details.
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your@mail.com"






Warning



Do not skip this step. It is easy to overlook, because nothing goes wrong until the first time you try to commit, and then Git refuses with an error message. Setting both values now saves you that error in week 2, when everybody is committing for the first time at once.




6. Create a GitHub account
If you do not already have one, create a free GitHub account. GitHub lets you store repositories online, collaborate, and reach your work from anywhere. We use it to distribute all course materials.


7. Check Quarto
Quarto is the publishing system that turns a .qmd file into HTML, PDF or slides, running your R code as it goes. Every artefact in this course, including this page, is a Quarto document.
Positron ships with Quarto, so if you installed Positron in step 2 you already have it. Confirm it from the Terminal:
quarto --version


8. Install TinyTeX
To render PDF output, Quarto needs a LaTeX engine. Let Quarto install and manage a small one for you, from the Terminal:
quarto install tinytex
Now continue with Section 10, which is the same on every operating system.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Install the R packages
This step is identical on Windows and macOS.
R packages are bundles of functions, data and documentation that extend R. You install a package once, and load it in each session where you need it. Table 1 lists what this course uses and why.



Table 1: The R packages this course uses, and what each one is for. Install them all before the first session. LaTeX is not on this list, because quarto install tinytex in step 8 already handled it.










Package
What it is
Why we use it




tidyverse
A collection of packages for data manipulation, visualisation and analysis, including dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr and readr.
A consistent framework for cleaning, exploring and visualising data. The backbone of nearly every script in the course.


here
Builds file paths from the project root.
Makes a project run on any machine, not just the one it was written on. Used for every path in this course.


brms
Fits Bayesian regression models with familiar R formula syntax, on top of Stan.
Our main modelling tool, from simple regression to multilevel models, without writing Stan code directly.


posterior
Tools for handling and summarising posterior draws.
Provides the convergence diagnostics we read after every fit.


bayesplot
Plots for Bayesian model checking and diagnostics.
Trace plots and posterior predictive checks, steps 6a and 6b of the workflow.


marginaleffects
Computes marginal effects and predictions from fitted models.
How we turn coefficients into interpretable quantities of interest.


ggpubr
Publication-ready ggplot2 themes.
Supplies theme_pubr(), the default theme for every figure in the course.


patchwork
Combines several plots into one figure.
For multi-panel figures.


modelsummary
Formats model output into tables.
Regression tables that can go straight into a report.


knitr
The engine that runs the R code inside a Quarto document.
Also provides kable() for computed tables.






How to install. In Positron, find the Console (see Figure 1), start an R session if one is not running already, and run:
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "here", "brms", "posterior", "bayesplot",
  "marginaleffects", "ggpubr", "patchwork", "modelsummary",
  "knitr"
))






Note



This will take a while, and that is expected. brms compiles C++ code during installation, so it is much slower than the others. Start it when you have time to leave it running.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Great, you made it






Tip



That was a lot, and you got through it. You now have a research toolchain on your machine that is genuinely the same one used for published empirical work. Nothing more is required before the first session.


If something did not work, do not spend an evening fighting it alone. Bring it to the first session, or email me beforehand with the exact error message, and we will sort it out together. Setup problems are common, they are almost always quick to fix once someone has seen them before, and this is precisely why the guide asks you to install early.

title: Getting started: installation guide
text:
Submitting your work

Open the homework link on the Schedule. It opens GitHub’s new-repository page, already filled in from the week’s template repo.
Check the Owner dropdown before you create anything. It must read qmir-2026-fall.
Replace USERNAME in the repository name with your own GitHub username, and leave the rest of the name as it is.
Do your work in that repo, commit, and push. Rendering the PDF and pushing is your submission.







Important



Two fields decide whether your work counts: Owner and name.
The Owner must be the course organisation qmir-2026-fall. The link pre-selects it, but the dropdown is editable and GitHub’s own default is your personal account. A repo created on your personal account is invisible to the tracker, no matter what is in it.
The name must be exactly hw-NN-<username>, with your own GitHub username and a zero-padded week number, for example hw-03-jdoe.








Note



The organisation only shows up in the Owner dropdown once you have joined it. You get an email invitation at the start of the term. Accept it before the first homework is due, and reload the page if the dropdown still offers only your own account.








Tip



Opt in to individual feedback with one file. Add an open-source license.md to your submission repo and an AI reads your work alongside the sample solution, then writes feedback back into the repo. See the Syllabus.

text:
Where today fits
Today starts step 2, the data summary. Every data summary you will write this term is a pipeline like the one we build today.





Table 1: The 8-step Bayesian workflow. Every homework exercises the steps introduced so far, cumulatively, and the exam runs all eight end to end.










#
Step
What you produce




1
Estimand
The quantity you want to learn about, stated precisely as a target before any model is fitted.


2
Data summary
The data described: measurement, coverage, obvious issues.


3
Formal model
Likelihood and priors written down, the generative model.


4
Prior predictive check
Simulate from the priors, confirm they imply plausible data.


5
Fit
Estimate with brms, weakly-informative priors by default.


6a
MCMC diagnostics
R-hat, ESS, divergences, trace plots. Did sampling work?


6b
Posterior predictive check
Does the fitted model reproduce key features of the data?


7
Interpretation
Answer the estimand on the outcome scale, with uncertainty.


8
Limitations
What the analysis can and cannot support, threats and next steps.








One minute. Point at step 2 only.

Cell options you have met

Two minutes, no practice. They used label, echo, eval and error in hw-03. Point at include, message, warning and the two captions as the new ones.





Table 2: The cell options this course uses, one #| line each at the top of a cell. Set under execute: in the YAML header, an option applies to every cell instead.





Option
What it does




label: my-name
Names the cell. Unique, and required.


echo: false
Runs the code, hides it, shows the result.


eval: false
Shows the code, does not run it.


include: false
Runs the code, shows nothing at all.


error: true
Shows an error and keeps rendering.


message: false
Hides messages, such as package startup text.


warning: false
Hides warnings.


fig-cap: "..."
Captions a figure, with a fig- label.


tbl-cap: "..."
Captions a table, with a tbl- label.

Layer
The message looks like

R

Your prose: a special character such as %, &, $ or a stray \.

Only the first error counts. Scroll up to the first message, fix that, and render again.

Packages: functions other people wrote

Last week you wrote your own function. A package is a bundle of functions, their help pages, and sometimes data, that someone wrote and shared.


R itself ships with the base packages: mean(), round(), data.frame().
CRAN, R’s package archive, holds more than 20,000 more, checked and free.
Nearly every method in this course lives in a package: dplyr today, ggplot2 next week, brms later.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
text:
Install once, load every session


Install downloads the package to your computer. Once, in the console.

install.packages("gapminder")


Load makes its functions available. Every session, at the top of your .qmd.

library(gapminder) # demo data



Like an app on your phone: you install it once, and you open it every time you use it.






Important


install.packages() never goes into a .qmd. It would reinstall on every render, and Quarto refuses to run it anyway.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
section: Quarto stops when a package is missing
text:
Quarto stops when a package is missing
If a library() call names a package that is not installed, the render stops at that cell:
Error in `library()`:
! there is no package called 'gapminder'
Quitting from hw-04.qmd:6-10 [setup]


That is an R error, reported through Quarto.
The fix is in the console, not in the document: install.packages("gapminder"), then render again.
It also happens when the name is misspelled: library(gapmindr) gives the same message.


This is the most common first-render failure on a new laptop. Everybody who installed a package in a different R version meets it once.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
text:
package::function()
:: names the package a function comes from.

gapminder::gapminder |> nrow()

[1] 1704



Three reasons when it can be useful:

Clarity: the reader sees where a function lives.
No library() needed for a one-off call, such as readxl::read_excel().
Name clashes: two packages can both have a filter(). library(tidyverse) tells you which one wins: ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter().

?dplyr::filter opens the help page of that exact function. Most packages also have good online documentation, such as dplyr.tidyverse.org.






Tip


Rule of thumb: more than three calls, load the package. Once you use a package’s functions more than three times, add a library() line to your setup cell instead of repeating package:: every time.

The tidyverse is a family of packages built on one shared philosophy:


Tidy data in, tidy data out: every function takes a table and returns a table.

Functions are verbs: filter(), select() and summarise() read like what they do.
Written for humans: consistent names and arguments, so learning one package teaches you the next.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
text:
The dplyr verbs






Table 10: The core dplyr verbs covered today. Each takes a table and returns a table, so they chain into one pipeline.





Verb
What it does




filter()
Keep rows that meet a condition


slice()
Keep rows by position


select()
Keep or drop columns


mutate()
Create new columns or change old ones


arrange()
Sort rows


left_join()
Add columns from another table


count()
Count rows per value of a column


group_by()
Split rows into groups


summarise()
Summary statistics, such as a mean, per group









Every verb:

takes a table first, so it pipes
names columns without quotes and without $
returns a new table and leaves the old one unchanged


We build one pipeline, one verb at a time. The highlighted line is the new one.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
text:
Four ways to join
A join combines two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as country.




Table 11: The four joins of dplyr. They differ only in which rows survive when a key has no partner in the other table.









Join
Keeps




left_join(x, y)
Every row of x, with the matching columns of y, and NA where y has no match


right_join(x, y)
Every row of y, with the matching columns of x, and NA where x has no match


inner_join(x, y)
Only the rows that match in both tables


full_join(x, y)
Every row of both tables, and NA wherever there is no match














Tip


In practice, left_join() is nearly always the one you want. Your main tibble sits on the left, and the join adds information to it from a second table. No row of your main data is lost, so it is the only join we practise today.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
section: Practice: from a question to an answer
text:
Practice: from a question to an answer

Eight minutes. Walk the room. Push pairs to run the pipeline after every line, not only at the end.

The question. In 2007, did European countries inside the EU live longer, and were they richer, than those outside?
Do this now. With gapminder and eu_members only, build one pipeline that returns one row per group, with the number of countries, the mean life expectancy and the mean GDP per capita.

Hints:

After the join, a country is a member in 2007 if it joined in 2007 or earlier: eu_member = !is.na(accession_date) & year(accession_date) <= 2007. year() comes from lubridate, loaded with the tidyverse.
Why not just !is.na(accession_date)? Croatia is in the file, but joined in 2013.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
text:
The whole pipeline

eu_2007 <- gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Europe", year == 2007) |> # rows
  left_join(eu_members, by = "country") |> # add a table
  mutate(
    eu_member = !is.na(accession_date) & year(accession_date) <= 2007
  ) |> # new column
  group_by(eu_member) |> # groups
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_life = mean(lifeExp),
    mean_gdppc = mean(gdpPercap)
  ) # one row per group
eu_2007

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  eu_member     n mean_life mean_gdppc
  <lgl>     <int>     <dbl>      <dbl>
1 FALSE         9      76.8     19838.
2 TRUE         21      78.0     27290.









Important


Pipelines are powerful, so test them at every step. Run the pipeline after each new line and look at what it returns: how many rows, which columns, any NAs? A pipeline you have not checked step by step can be wrong without a single error message.

title: Week 4: The tidyverse
text:
The answer
Yes, on both counts, but by very different margins.

The 21 EU members lived 1.2 years longer on average than the 9 countries outside: 78.0 against 76.8.
Their mean GDP per capita was about 7,000 US dollars higher.








Note


A mean hides who is in the group. The countries outside mix Norway and Switzerland, among the richest in the data, with Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina. And a difference between groups says nothing yet about whether membership caused it: that is step 8, the limitations.
